short.en: Every way in has a cost

t.en: only allowed swapping letters. But typing also adds and drops letters, so real correction has to answer: what is the fewest steps that turn one word into another?
Each step does exactly one thing: delete a letter, insert a letter, or replace one letter with another. For example, CAT → CUT takes just 1 step: replace A with U.

It’s an alignment table again: the rows are the original word, the columns the target word. Each cell records the fewest steps that turn “the first few letters of the original” into “the first few letters of the target”. Each of the three neighbors has a meaning:

Every way in has its own cost: how many extra steps it takes to come that way. Deleting, inserting and replacing each cost 1 step; when the two letters match, coming from the up-left lets you keep the letter for free.

This time, row 0 and column 0 have no ready-made numbers; the circuit has to compute them too. Think: how many steps turn the first 3 letters of the original into an empty word? And when both words are empty?

goal.en: Each step deletes, inserts or replaces one letter. Build the typo-fixing circuit and work out the fewest steps that turn one word into another.

how.en: This board needs quite a few components. Once you pass, look at the exact edits the table traces back.

body.en: The fewest steps that turn one word into another is called the edit distance. Autocorrect, a search engine’s “Did you mean…?” and the analysis of gene mutations all rely on it.

Compared with , the table’s shape didn’t change at all: you just gave every way in a cost and took the min. Even the row and column along the edges were computed by the same circuit. The same alignment table with a different circuit board answers a different question.

note.en: Edit distance: delete, insert and replace each cost 1, a matching letter can be kept for free, and you take the min.

hints.en: Deleting a letter (from above), inserting one (from the left) and replacing one (from the up-left) each cost 1 more step. To get the fewest steps, how should these three ways in be combined?
When the two letters match you can just keep it: come from the up-left at no cost. Use a Pass gate with “letters match” as its condition and “up-left” as its number.
The start (both words empty) is 0 steps: let a 0 through on “is start”. Finally, wire all three paths into another “min” Merger.
